'''Stanton Terry Friedman''' (July 29, 1934&nbsp;– May 13, 2019)<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/stanton-friedman-ufologist-dead-1.5135588|title=Stanton Friedman, famed UFO researcher, dead at 84|publisher=[[CBC News]]}}</ref> was an American–Canadian [[nuclear physicist]] and professional [[Ufology|ufologist]] who was based in [[Fredericton]], New Brunswick, Canada.

==Early life==
Born in [[Elizabeth, New Jersey]], Friedman was raised in nearby [[Linden, New Jersey|Linden]] and graduated from [[Linden High School (New Jersey)|Linden High School]] in 1951; he attended [[Rutgers University]] and then transferred to the [[University of Chicago]], earning a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1955 and a master's degree in [[nuclear physics]] in 1956.<ref>[https://vault.fbi.gov/stanton-terrance-friedman/stanton-terrance-friedman-part-01-of-01#page=20 File on Stanton Friedman], [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]]. Accessed April 13, 2022. "Stanton Terry Friedman was born on July 29, 1934, at Elizabeth, New Jersey, he is the son of Louis and Florence Friedman. Stanton Friedman spent his childhood in Linden, New Jersey and attended Linden High School from 1947–1951. He attended college at Rutgers University from 1951—1953 and then the University of Chicago during the years 1953–1956."</ref><ref>Story, Ronald (ed.), ''The Encyclopedia of UFOs''; Garden City: Doubleday & Company, Inc, 1980, {{ISBN|0385136773}}</ref>

=== Career in nuclear physics ===
Friedman was employed for 14 years as a nuclear physicist for such companies as [[General Electric]] (1956–1959), [[Aerojet|Aerojet General Nucleonics]] (1959–1963), [[General Motors]] (1963–1966), [[Northrop Grumman Electronic Systems|Westinghouse]] (1966–1968), [[TRW Inc.|TRW Systems]] (1969–1970), and [[McDonnell Douglas]], where he worked on advanced, classified programs on nuclear aircraft, fission and fusion rockets, and compact nuclear power plants for space applications.<ref name="FSS"/> Since the 1980s, he consulted for the [[radon]]-detection industry. Friedman's professional affiliations included the [[American Nuclear Society]], the [[American Physical Society]], the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]], and [[AFTRA]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2014}}

===UFO investigations and advocacy===
In 1970, Friedman left full-time employment as a physicist to pursue the scientific investigation of [[unidentified flying object]]s (UFOs). Since then, he gave lectures at more than 600 colleges and to more than 100 professional groups in 50 states, 10 provinces, and 19 countries outside the US.<ref name="FSS"/> Additionally, he worked as a consultant on the topic. He published more than 80 UFO-related papers and appeared on many radio and television programs.<ref name="FSS">Friedman, S. (2008). ''Flying Saucers and Science: A Scientist Investigates the Mysteries of UFOs''. Franklin Lakes, NJ: New Page Books {{ISBN|978-1601630117}}</ref> He also provided written testimony to Congressional hearings and appeared twice at the [[United Nations]].<ref name="FSS"/><ref name="shgintro">{{Cite web |title=SHG – UFO Symposium 1968: Introduction By Jan L. Aldrich |url=http://www.project1947.com/shg/symposium/shgintro.html |website=project1947.com}}</ref>

Friedman consistently favored use of the term "[[flying saucer]]" in his work, saying "Flying saucers are, by definition, unidentified flying objects, but very few unidentified flying objects are flying saucers. I am interested in the latter, not the former."<ref name="FSS"/> He used to refer to himself as "The Flying Saucer Physicist", because of his degrees in [[nuclear physics]] and work on nuclear projects.<ref name="shgintro"/>

==Friedman's positions regarding UFO phenomena==
Friedman was the first civilian to document the site of the [[Roswell UFO incident]],<ref name="Star Phoenix">
{{Cite news |last=Pacholik |first=Barb |date=April 23, 2007 |title=UFO expert has little patience for 'nasty, noisy negativists' |url=http://www.canada.com/saskatoonstarphoenix/news/story.html?id=dd7048f8-9648-4cc0-8135-27d5ec8c7b9b |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924104919/http://www.canada.com/saskatoonstarphoenix/news/story.html?id=dd7048f8-9648-4cc0-8135-27d5ec8c7b9b |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=September 22, 2015 |newspaper=The Star Phoenix |location=Saskatoon, SK}}
</ref> and supported the hypothesis that it was a genuine crash of an extraterrestrial spacecraft.<ref name="Crash">Berliner, D. & Friedman, S.T. (2004). ''Crash at Corona: The U.S. Military Retrieval and Cover-up of A UFO''. Cosimo, Inc. {{ISBN|978-1931044899}}</ref> In 1968 Friedman told a committee of the [[United States House of Representatives]] that the evidence suggests that Earth is being visited by intelligently controlled extraterrestrial vehicles.<ref>{{Cite web |url = http://ncas.org/ufosymposium/friedman.html |title = Statement by Stanton T. Friedman |access-date = February 19, 2009 |date=January 2001 |publisher = National Capital Area Skeptics}}</ref> Friedman also stated he believed that [[UFO]] sightings were consistent with [[Magnetohydrodynamics|magnetohydrodynamic]] propulsion.

In 1996, after researching and [[fact checking]] the [[Majestic 12]] documents, Friedman said that there was no substantive grounds for dismissing their authenticity.<ref name="Friedman, S.T. 1996">Friedman, S.T. (1996). ''Top Secret/MAJIC: Operation Majestic-12 and the United States Government's UFO Cover-Up''. New York: Marlowe & Company. {{ISBN|978-1569243428}}</ref>

In 2004, on [[George Noory]]'s ''Coast to Coast'' radio show, Friedman debated [[Seth Shostak]], the [[SETI Institute]]'s Senior Astronomer. Like Friedman, Shostak also believes in the existence of intelligent life other than humans; however, unlike Friedman, he does not believe such life is now on Earth or is related to UFO sightings.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 21, 2004 |title=The Great UFO Debate |url=http://www.coasttocoastam.com/shows/2004/07/21.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318034745/http://www.coasttocoastam.com/shows/2004/07/21.html |archive-date=March 18, 2009 |access-date=February 19, 2009 |publisher=Premier Radio Networks}}</ref>

Friedman hypothesized that UFOs may originate from relatively nearby sunlike stars.<ref name="FSS"/>(p.&nbsp;217)

A piece of evidence that he often cited with respect to this hypothesis is the [[Barney and Betty Hill#Analyzing the star map|1964 star map]] drawn by alleged [[alien abduction|alien abductee]] [[Barney and Betty Hill|Betty Hill]] during a hypnosis session, which she said was shown to her during her abduction. [[Astronomer]] Marjorie Fish constructed a three-dimensional map of nearby sun-like stars and claimed a good match from the perspective of [[Zeta Reticuli#Zeta Reticuli in ufology|Zeta Reticuli]], about 39 light-years distant. The fit of the Hill/Fish star maps was hotly debated in the December 1974 edition of [[Astronomy (magazine)|''Astronomy'' magazine]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dickinson |first=Terence |title=The Zeta Reticuli Incident |url=http://www.nicap.org/articles/hillzeta.htm |access-date=February 19, 2009 |publisher=The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena (NICAP)}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wright |first=Kenneth F. |date=April 10, 2000 |title=Zeta Reticuli Incident |url=http://www.gravitywarpdrive.com/Zeta_Reticuli_Incident.htm |access-date=February 19, 2009}}</ref> with Friedman and others defending the statistical validity of the match.

===SETI===
Friedman stated strong views against [[search for extraterrestrial intelligence]] (SETI) research. Friedman contested the implicit premise of SETI that there has been no extraterrestrial visitation of the planet, because it was his claim that SETI was seeking only signals, not extraterrestrial intelligence or beings. He maintained that the prominence and widespread public claims of those involved with SETI have tended to prevent serious research of UFOs, including research by journalists.<ref name="FSS"/>(p.&nbsp;129)

Friedman was a classmate of [[Carl Sagan]] at the University of Chicago. Friedman criticized Sagan, a proponent of SETI, for ignoring empirical evidence, such as "600-plus ''unknowns''" of ''[[Project Blue Book#Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14|Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14]]''. Friedman argued that these empirical data directly contradict Sagan's claim in ''Other Worlds'' that the "reliable cases are uninteresting and the interesting cases are unreliable". Specifically, Friedman referred to a table in ''Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14'' that he said "shows that the better the quality of the sighting, the more likely it was to be an 'unknown', and the less likely it was to be listed as containing 'insufficient information'"<ref name="FSS"/>(p.&nbsp;42).

===Public and scientific opinion===
Friedman said of the response to his talks, "I know that most people are unfamiliar with the several large-scale scientific studies&nbsp;... because I ask, after I show a slide and ask about each one, 'How many here have read this?' Typically, it is only one or two percent". He said that a talk he gave to Canadian journalists in [[Saint John, New Brunswick]], caused the attitudes of the journalists to change, because "...&nbsp;attendees had had no idea there was so much solid information, as opposed to the tabloid nonsense they thought was the primary source of UFO data". (p.&nbsp;202)<ref name="FSS"/>

Friedman argued that the majority of people believe UFOs exist and at least some groups of scientists do as well. Friedman (2008) referred to the following data in support of his position:<ref name="Friedman, S.T. 1996"/>
* [[Gallup (company)#Gallup Poll|Gallup Polls]] between 1966 and 1987 asked respondents the question: "Are UFOs something real, or just people's imagination?" Of those who took a position one way or the other, 61%, 64%, 68%, and 60% took the position they are real in 1966, 1977, 1978, and 1987, respectively.
* With respect to scientists, a poll was taken by Industrial Research and Development in 1971 and 1979. Of the respondents who took a position, 64% and 69% stated they believed UFOs either probably or definitely exist. Of this subgroup, 32% and 44% considered their origin to be Outer Space in 1971 and 1979, respectively. Of the rest of this subgroup, approximately half believed them to be natural phenomena and half were "undecided".
* [[Peter A. Sturrock|Peter Sturrock]] also polled the membership of the American Astronomical Society and found that "the greater the amount of time one spent on reading UFO-related material, the more likely one is to accept their reality" (p.&nbsp;210).<ref name="FSS"/>

==Criticisms and controversies==
{{For |his criticism of the [[Search for extraterrestrial intelligence]]|Search for extraterrestrial intelligence#Stanton Friedman}}
Friedman was outspoken in his articulation of positions and in his criticism of UFO [[debunker]]s, often stating he was not an "apologist ufologist". His positions are regarded as controversial in mainstream science and media, but Friedman claimed to have received little opposition at his many lectures, most of which were at colleges and universities, many to engineering societies and other groups of physicists<ref name="FSS"/> (p.&nbsp;24). He had a number of debates in the mainstream media, including one with UFO skeptic [[Michael Shermer]] on [[CNN]].

Friedman was criticized both by skeptics and other Roswell researchers for taking the position that there are no substantive grounds for dismissing the authenticity of some ''Majestic 12'' documents although Friedman was the first to provide evidence that some of the documents are clearly hoaxes. For example, he showed that a supposed memo from [[Roscoe H. Hillenkoetter|Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter]] to [[President Truman]], dated February 17, 1948, was actually the emulation of a letter from [[George C. Marshall|Marshall]] to Roosevelt that was featured in the book ''The American MAGIC''. Friedman researched the MJ-12 documents since first becoming aware of them from [[Bill Moore (ufologist)|William Moore]] and Jaime Shandera in 1984.<ref name="FSS"/><ref>''Top Secret/MAJIC: Operation Majestic-12 and the United States Government's UFO Cover-Up''. New York: Marlowe & Company. {{ISBN|978-1569243428}}</ref> He addressed criticisms of the original documents in both sources. As an example, [[Philip J. Klass]] claimed lexicographic inconsistencies based on the use of Pica typeface in the Cutler-Twining memo and offered $100, in a challenge to Friedman, for each legitimate example of the use of the same style and size Pica type as used in the memo. Friedman provided 14 examples and was paid $1000 by Klass.<ref name="FSS"/>

==Personal life==
Friedman was [[Ashkenazi Jews|Ashkenazi Jewish]]. He was married twice. His first wife was Susie Virginia Porter, with whom he adopted three children, but they divorced in April 1974.<ref>California, Divorce Index, 1966–1984; Los Angeles April 1974.</ref> He had one daughter with his second wife, Stella Marilyn Kimball.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Obituary of Stella Marilyn Friedman {{!}} York Funeral Home |url=https://yorkfh.com/tribute/details/16993/Stella-Friedman/obituary.html |access-date=March 7, 2024 |website=yorkfh.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Friedman relocated to Marilyn's native [[Fredericton]], New Brunswick in the early 1980s.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gibson |first=Lydialyle |date=September–October 2011 |title=Science? Fiction? |url=http://mag.uchicago.edu/science-medicine/science-fiction |access-date=December 30, 2015 |work=University of Chicago Magazine |publisher=[[University of Chicago]]}}</ref> Friedman donated his records to the [[Provincial Archives of New Brunswick]] in the months leading up to his death.<ref>{{cite news |title=Archivist delighted to comb through mountain of late UFO researcher's records |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/provincial-archives-stanton-friedman-records-1.5315664 |access-date=January 6, 2024 |work=[[CBC News]] |date=October 13, 2019}}</ref>

On May 13, 2019, Friedman died of a heart attack at the [[Toronto Pearson Airport]] while traveling home from a speaking engagement in [[Columbus, Ohio]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sandomir |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Sandomir |date=May 21, 2019 |title=Stanton T. Friedman, Scientist Who Tracked U.F.O.s, Dies at 84 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/21/obituaries/stanton-friedman-dead.html |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>
